summaries.example: Imagine two students see a classmate drop a lunchbox. One helps because they care about the classmate. Another helps because they think being helpful will earn a reward. Psychological egoism asks whether every action is ultimately done for the helper’s own welfare. Some philosophers say yes, but critics ask whether caring about another person can sometimes be a real goal by itself.
summaries.summary: Egoism is the idea that the self has a special place in human action. The entry separates three views. Psychological egoism is a claim about motivation: it says that each person ultimately aims at their own welfare. Ethical egoism is a moral claim: it says each person ought to do what best serves their own self-interest. Rational egoism is a broader claim about reasons: it says each person ought to do what best serves their own self-interest, even when the question is not specifically moral. The article explains that “welfare” might mean pleasure, getting what one desires, or having valuable things such as knowledge. It examines whether apparently caring actions can really be selfish, and whether cooperation gives us reasons to care about others. It also presents objections: egoism may treat concern for oneself as arbitrary, may ignore reasons such as promises or another person’s danger, and may have trouble explaining why we should care more about our own future than about other people. The entry’s conclusion is cautious: psychological egoism has weak prospects, while rational egoism remains a serious but disputed position.
key_ideas: Egoism can describe how people act, or it can tell people what they ought to do.
Psychological egoism says people always have their own welfare as their deepest aim, but apparent self-sacrifice creates a serious challenge.
Ethical egoism concerns moral rules, while rational egoism concerns reasons for action more generally.
Helping others may sometimes be good for us, but that does not automatically show that helping is always selfish.
The entry considers arguments from cooperation, personal preferences, future selves, and evidence about human behavior.
summaries.why_it_matters: Egoism helps us ask an important question: when we choose, should we think only about what happens to us? It also helps separate three different questions—what people do, what is morally right, and what people have reason to do. Understanding these differences can prevent arguments from becoming confused. The topic matters whenever we think about kindness, promises, fairness, sacrifice, and the reasons we have to care about other people.

important_terms.definition: A view about what motivates people. Psychological egoism says that each person’s ultimate aim is their own welfare.
How well a person is doing, such as having pleasure, knowledge, good character, or satisfied desires.
A view about what people morally ought to do. Ethical egoism says a person should do what best serves their own self-interest.
A view about what a person has most reason to do, whether or not the reason is moral. Rational egoism focuses on maximizing one’s own self-interest.
What benefits or helps a person. Philosophers disagree about whether it means pleasure, getting what one wants, or having valuable things such as knowledge.

questions_to_think_about: Can someone help another person simply because they want that person to be safe?
If helping feels good, does that make the help selfish?
Would people cooperate if they never expected a reward or punishment?
Is doing what is best for yourself always the same as doing what is right?

summaries.example: Suppose a student can spend an afternoon preparing for a scholarship exam or helping a stranger whose car has broken down. An ethical egoist asks which choice best advances the student’s self-interest as a moral matter. A rational egoist asks which choice the student has most reason to make, even apart from morality. A psychological egoist asks a different question: whatever the student chooses, is the ultimate motivation necessarily the student’s own welfare? The student might help because of compassion, duty, expected gratitude, guilt avoidance, or some combination. The example shows why a theory about motivation does not automatically establish a theory about what one ought to do.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry treats egoism as a family of positions rather than a single thesis. Psychological egoism is descriptive: it claims that each person’s ultimate aim is their own welfare. Its plausibility depends partly on what welfare means. Desire-based accounts identify welfare with the satisfaction of desires, objective accounts appeal to goods such as knowledge or virtue, and hybrid accounts combine these approaches. Psychological egoism can reinterpret helping as a route to pleasure, power, guilt avoidance, or another benefit. Critics reply that this may fail to explain genuine other-regarding motivation, and that defining self-interest as satisfaction of all preferences makes the theory empty rather than empirically informative. The entry discusses experimental and evolutionary arguments for altruistic motivation, while also noting limitations in those arguments. Ethical egoism is normative in a specifically moral sense: each agent ought to maximize their own self-interest. It may explain ordinary cooperation, but appears to diverge from common moral judgments in cases involving non-reciprocal aid, unequal benefits, or great sacrifice. It also faces objections about publicity, consistency, and whether it qualifies as a moral theory. Rational egoism makes a wider normative claim about reasons for action. It confronts the instrumental theory of rationality, the arbitrariness of privileging oneself, alternatives based on present aims, arguments from personal identity, and evolutionary debunking arguments. The entry concludes that psychological egoism has poor prospects, while rational egoism remains worth taking seriously but is surrounded by substantial unresolved objections.
key_ideas: The central distinction is between descriptive egoism, which concerns motivation, and normative egoism, which concerns what one ought to do.
Psychological egoism can explain some apparently altruistic actions as means to welfare, but critics argue that some actions seem aimed at others’ good or at duty itself.

If self-interest is defined as satisfaction of every preference, psychological egoism risks becoming trivial: every intentional action would count as self-interested. That would fail to distinguish selfish from unselfish choices.

Ethical egoism may support cooperation because trust, friendship, and defense benefit each person, yet this does not clearly justify helping people who cannot reciprocate or making extreme sacrifices.
Rational egoism faces the objection that favoring oneself may be no less arbitrary than favoring a random group, such as people with a certain eye color.

Challenges involving present desires, future persons, personal identity, and evolutionary explanations suggest that self-interest may not be the only source of reasons, though the entry does not treat these challenges as conclusive.
summaries.why_it_matters: Egoism sits at the intersection of moral psychology, ethics, and theories of practical reason. It forces a separation between a claim about what motivates us and a claim about what is justified. That separation matters because even if people often act from self-interest, it would not by itself follow that they ought to do so. The debate also tests ideas about altruism, moral obligation, cooperation, future-oriented concern, and the authority of reasons. Studying egoism therefore clarifies both the reach and the limits of self-interest as a guide to action.

important_terms.definition: A descriptive theory claiming that each person has only one ultimate aim: their own welfare. It allows that people may pursue other things as means to that welfare.
A normative theory claiming that an action is morally required exactly when, and because, it maximizes the agent’s self-interest.
A normative theory about what one ought to do or has reason to do, without limiting the relevant “ought” to moral obligation.
A person’s welfare or well-being. Accounts may identify it with satisfied desires, independently valuable states such as knowledge or virtue, or a combination.
The view that rational action should maximize the satisfaction of one’s preferences. It can conflict with rational egoism when preferences are other-regarding.
A desire for something as an end in itself, rather than merely as a tool for gaining something else.
The concern that a principle gives no adequate reason for treating one case differently from another. Rational egoism faces this worry about privileging oneself.

The connection among memories, traits, intentions, and other psychological features across time. Some arguments use these connections to question whether identity alone grounds special concern for one’s future.

questions_to_think_about: Does explaining why someone helps—perhaps through guilt or reward—show that the help was selfish, or only that it had a possible explanation?
Can cooperation based on mutual advantage produce all ordinary moral duties, including duties toward people who cannot help or punish us?
Why should a person’s own welfare matter more than another person’s welfare? What would count as a non-arbitrary answer?
If a future person has many of my memories and traits but is not strictly identical with me, do I have a special reason to care about that person?
Could a theory guide and criticize choices even when people are not motivated to follow it?

summaries.example: A student promises to share notes with a classmate who missed school. Keeping the promise takes time, but it may preserve trust and lead to future help. An ethical egoist might say the student should keep the promise because doing so serves the student’s self-interest through cooperation. But what if the classmate cannot ever return the favor and nobody else will know whether the promise was kept? The cooperation argument becomes weaker. A different question is whether the student might still have a moral reason to help simply because the classmate needs the notes.
summaries.summary: The entry explains that egoism can be a description of human motivation or a rule about what people ought to do. Psychological egoism says that a person’s ultimate aim is always their own welfare. To assess it, we need an account of welfare: it might be pleasure, the satisfaction of desires, valuable conditions such as knowledge or virtue, or a mixture. Psychological egoists can explain apparent generosity by saying that helping brings a personal benefit, such as happiness, relief from guilt, or a sense of power. Critics argue that some actions seem to aim directly at another person’s good or at doing one’s duty. They also point out that if every intentional action satisfies some preference, then the theory may simply label all action self-interested instead of making a testable claim. Ethical egoism says that morality requires maximizing one’s own self-interest. It can explain why people should often cooperate, since trust and friendship benefit everyone, but it may not explain duties toward people who cannot repay or punish us. Rational egoism makes a broader claim about what one has reason to do. It faces the worry that giving special importance to oneself may be arbitrary, as well as challenges from theories based on present desires and from questions about why we should care especially about future versions of ourselves. The entry treats psychological egoism as especially doubtful and rational egoism as a position that remains contested.
key_ideas: Psychological egoism describes motivation; ethical and rational egoism prescribe what people ought to do.

A person can want to help someone else, and an egoist may still argue that this desire somehow serves the person’s welfare. The disagreement is about whether concern for others can be an ultimate goal.
If every satisfied preference counts as self-interest, psychological egoism may become true merely by definition and lose its power to explain behavior.
Ethical egoism can support many cooperative actions because people need one another, but it may not support aid when there is no chance of cooperation or retaliation.
Rational egoism must explain why one’s own welfare should receive special weight rather than being dismissed as an unsupported preference.
The entry presents arguments on both sides and ends with stronger doubts about psychological egoism than about rational egoism.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps us distinguish behavior, morality, and rational choice. Someone may act kindly because of compassion, habit, duty, expected reward, or several motives at once. Even if self-interest is one motive, that does not settle whether self-interest should be the standard for right action. Egoism also raises practical questions about trust and cooperation: are we kind only because it pays, or can another person’s needs give us a reason on their own? These questions appear in friendships, promises, fairness, and decisions about sacrifice.

important_terms.definition: A claim about how people are motivated. Psychological egoism says every person’s deepest or ultimate aim is their own welfare.
A claim about morality. Ethical egoism says each person morally ought to choose the action that maximizes their own self-interest.
A claim about reasons for action in general, not only moral duties. Rational egoism says one ought to maximize one’s own self-interest.
What contributes to a person’s well-being. It might involve pleasure, satisfied desires, knowledge, virtue, or more than one of these.
A reason that supports an action because the action helps achieve some goal, rather than because the action is valuable as an end.
A desire for something for its own sake, not merely because it leads to a personal benefit.
The idea that a rule or choice is unsupported because it treats one case as special without explaining why.
The benefits people can gain by working together, such as trust, friendship, or protection. Egoist arguments often appeal to these benefits.

questions_to_think_about: Is an action selfish if it makes the person feel good, even when the person’s main goal was helping someone else?
Does the need for cooperation explain why we should keep promises only when others can respond?
What makes caring about yourself different from caring about a favorite group?
Can a person have reasons based on duty, promises, or another person’s needs as well as reasons based on self-interest?
